transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-05 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kumar (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Kestrel ML Eng), Nina Gomez (Kestrel Infra), Marcus Rey (Kestrel CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough): go over last week's TTFT numbers, dig into kernel choice diffs, decide next benchmark matrix, check streaming quality for longer sequences, confirm infra/VPC steps.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Alex from Redwood here. Quick round — Priya I think you have the kernel slides?
[00:12] Priya Kumar: Yeah, I pulled the latest timings. Uh, quick note: some of the earlier numbers we shared were single-run; today we have median and stdev across 5 runs on the dedicated nodes.
[00:25] Jordan Lee: Awesome, that's helpful. We mainly care about TTFT for short prompts (20-80 tokens) and streaming behaviour for up to 512 seq len.
[00:35] Marcus Rey: And just to reiterate, our SLO is P50 < 150ms for our chat starter flows. P95 we'd like sub-300ms if possible.
[00:46] Nina Gomez: I'll add, our infra limits are 16GB per GPU for the pilot, so quantization matters, and we have to track memory and kernel tradeoffs.
[00:58] Priya Kumar: Great, slide one: TTFT summary. We ran two kernel paths — fused-attention optimized kernels vs the more generic transformer kernels. For short sequences fused gave ~1.6x improvement on TTFT at batch=1, seq=64. However for long sequences (seq>256) the gap narrows due to memory bandwidth and matmul bottleneck.
[01:20] Jordan Lee: Do you have exact numbers for batch=1 vs batch=4? We saw weird regressions when batching was >2 on our test harness.
[01:29] Priya Kumar: Yes — batch=1 P50 was 120ms on fused, generic 190ms. Batch=4 on fused goes to 160ms per request if you amortize, but TTFT increases of course since batching waits for more tokens to coalesce. For short-latency flows we recommend batch=1 with prefix caching.
[01:49] Alex Chen: Quick interruption — when you say prefix caching, are we talking about KV cache persist between requests for the same session, or more like prefix-snapshotting?
[01:58] Priya Kumar: KV cache per session — yes. We saw 20-30% improvement on repeated-turn flows. But note you need sticky routing to maintain the cache benefits.
[02:08] Nina Gomez: That's important — our load balancer currently doesn't do sticky sessions; would Redwood's hosted route or dedicated pool make that easier?
[02:16] Alex Chen: For the pilot, dedicated pools let us guarantee stickiness and also let us pin fused kernels at serving time. For hosted we have session affinity options but they're less deterministic.
[02:28] Marcus Rey: On the streaming side — our UX requires early token arrival, so TTFT *and* first streaming packet is critical. Any insights there?
[02:37] Priya Kumar: Streaming path is interesting: fused kernels reduce compute for the first token but the network/serialization path becomes visible. We profiled the code-path: there's about 8-12ms in our stack for chunking + gRPC serialization once the tokens start streaming. For P50 that's fine, for P95 we need to tune message sizes and the gRPC compression.
[02:57] Jordan Lee: Are those 8-12ms numbers with gzip enabled? On our side gzip adds CPU overhead, maybe we should try no compression for short bursts.
[03:05] Priya Kumar: We tested both. Without compression the network bytes are larger but serialization is ~5ms faster. There is a tradeoff on cost. We'll put both in the benchmark CSV.
[03:15] Alex Chen: Can we jump to the kernel traces you mentioned? I remember you flagged one fused kernel path that regresses at seq=512.
[03:23] Priya Kumar: Right — at seq=512 the attention batching reorders memory and we hit a half-precision reduction path that causes extra copies. The fused kernel still wins on 64/128, but at 512 the generic path is similarly performant or slightly better depending on memory layout. We think a small kernel tweak can help, but it's non-trivial.
[03:44] Nina Gomez: That matches what we saw — long sequences blow out memory and we get OOMs if we don't quantize to int8. Any recommendations there?
[03:52] Priya Kumar: For 16GB GPUs, int8 quant plus a memory-aware kernel selection is our recommended approach. There's a small quality tradeoff; our Optimize team has baseline numbers. Also consider sequence slicing + streaming to avoid full-seq compute.
[04:06] Jordan Lee: Sequence slicing meaning chunking the 512 tokens into 128 windows and streaming each? Does that preserve context?
[04:15] Priya Kumar: You'd need to recompute cross-window context or carry a summarized context — that's an application-level tradeoff. For many chat UIs incremental prefix + KV cache is enough and cheaper.
[04:27] Alex Chen: Let's discuss the benchmark matrix we agreed to run. Priya?
[04:31] Priya Kumar: We propose to run: batch sizes 1, 4, 8; seq lengths 64, 128, 512; kernels fused vs generic; quant modes FP16 vs int8; streaming on/off. We'll capture TTFT, token-per-second, memory usage, and first-chunk latency.
[04:49] Marcus Rey: We'll need raw logs because our infra team will sanity-check the measurements against our noise profile.
[04:55] Priya Kumar: Yep — we'll provide raw traces and a CSV with median/stdev. Note though our env is Redwood-managed dedicated nodes; results will be close but might diverge slightly on your on-prem boxes.
[05:06] Nina Gomez: Why dedicated nodes? Is that because of kernel ABI or driver versions?
[05:12] Priya Kumar: Mostly driver and kernel flags. Some fused kernels depend on newer CUDA/cuBLAS kernels that are not available on older drivers. So driver mismatch can flip performance.
[05:22] Jordan Lee: OK good to know. We'll also validate on our k8s cluster with the same driver version.
[05:28] Alex Chen: There's a note about fallback policies — if fused kernel fails on some sequence we can route to generic kernel. That adds latency but keeps service healthy. Priya, does the runtime handle graceful fallback automatically?
[05:40] Priya Kumar: Yes the runtime has per-model kernel fallbacks. We instrument the tracing so you can see the fallback counts. It's configurable per-route.
[05:48] Jordan Lee: Can we see a dashboard with fallback counts and per-token cost? We're trying to balance cost/perf.
[05:55] Alex Chen: Redwood Console will show token-level cost and fallback metrics; we'll include a sample dashboard link in the follow-up.
[06:02] Nina Gomez: Security quick check — earlier we asked for KMS integration and SOC2 logs; any blockers?
[06:09] Alex Chen: No blockers. For Private deployment we support KMS/HSM integration and we export audit logs. For hosted you can enable customer-managed keys via our new KMS bridge. We'll attach the SOC2 security pack.
[06:20] Marcus Rey: Great. On pricing: if we go dedicated what's the rough delta vs hosted?
[06:26] Alex Chen: Dedicated is a monthly reserved capacity with lower unit token costs but an upfront commit. We'll send a comparative pricing sheet. Action item on me to upload it by Friday.
[06:35] Jordan Lee: Back to latency: are you confident we can hit our P95 sub-300ms with seq=64 and batch=1?
[06:42] Priya Kumar: Yes with fused kernels and prefix/KV caching plus sticky routing we have good confidence. We'll validate in the matrix. For seq=512 P95 will be higher; we'll measure streaming-first-chunk to see how UX feels.
[06:55] Nina Gomez: One blind spot: network egress on our cluster is variable — would that skew the streaming tests?
[07:01] Priya Kumar: It could. That's why we ask you to provide a representative test harness from your infra so we can run identical network conditions or you can run the Redwood Docker image and collect traces.
[07:11] Jordan Lee: We'll do that. We'll spin up the sample harness and run the 512 prompt set.
[07:16] Marcus Rey: Any concerns about model version pinning during rollout? We want canary then full.
[07:22] Alex Chen: Redwood supports canary rollouts and automatic fallback to earlier model versions if regressions are detected. We'll help you set the rollout thresholds.
[07:30] Priya Kumar: Also reminder: quantization can change output distribution slightly; pair evals with the rollout so you catch regressions.
[07:38] Jordan Lee: Good call. Ok wrapping to action items — Alex to share pricing and benchmark CSVs, Priya to run expanded kernel matrix, Nina to send network diagram, Jordan to upload prompts. Any other blockers?
[07:51] Marcus Rey: One ask — can Redwood run a short 2-hour focused run where we simulate 50 concurrent users to see queuing effects?
[07:59] Priya Kumar: Yes we can schedule that. It will be on dedicated infra to remove noisy neighbor variance. We'll propose times in the follow-up.
[08:07] Alex Chen: Cool. I'll set the follow-up for the week of Aug 12 for a deeper latency-only session.
[08:12] Nina Gomez: Thanks everyone — slight note, sometimes the transcript tool changes KV cache to K-V cash... so ignore small typos.
[08:20] (crosstalk) Jordan Lee: Thanks, bye.

End of meeting.
